title: Tosca
facts: Today’s matinee is the Met’s 1,017th Tosca. The very first was on 4 February 1901.
Host Ailyn Pérez knows this composer from the inside: she sang Puccini’s Mimì at the Met in 2016.
No overture: three loud, strident chords, Scarpia’s motif, then the fugitive Angelotti bursts in.
Freddie De Tommaso made his Met debut this month as Cavaradossi, opposite Lise Davidsen’s Tosca.
“Recondita armonia”: wait for the sustained high B flat, as the sacristan grumbles a counter-melody.
^Act\ I:\ Ma\ con\ quei\ cani\ …\ Eccellenza$
Patrick Carfizzi (Sacristan) and Christopher Job (Sciarrone) also sang this staging’s Met opening night, 31 Dec 2017.
Tosca arrives on her own motif. She’s suspicious, but the music paints her devotion and serenity.
The love duet “Qual’occhio” is Puccini at his most sensuous, with an almost erotic lyricism.
^Act\ I:\ Or\ lasciami\ al\ lavoro—Qua\ l'occhio\ al\ mondo$
Lise Davidsen won Operalia in 2015 and debuted at the Met in 2019, as Lisa in The Queen of Spades.
The sacristan and choirboys celebrate Napoleon’s “defeat”: almost the last carefree moments in the opera.
Scarpia enters on his menacing theme. Then the fugitive motif returns three times, louder each time.
Quinn Kelsey started in the Hawaii Opera Theatre chorus in 1991. His Met debut: Schaunard, in 2008.
Te Deum: Scarpia’s lustful reverie is sung right alongside the swelling chorus, then he joins the prayer.
McVicar’s staging premiered at the Met’s 2017 New Year’s Eve gala, co-produced with the Bavarian State Opera and La Scala.
That distant gavotte? Puccini adapted a student exercise by his late brother Michele, so he could “live again”.
Offstage, Tosca sings a cantata with the chorus, most likely Puccini’s own Cantata a Giove, a lost 1897 work.
News of Napoleon’s victory: Cavaradossi’s brief, ringing “Vittoria! Vittoria!” gives the torture scenes only partial relief.
Puccini thought “Vissi d’arte” was a mistake. He considered cutting it, since it held up the action.
^Act\ II:\ Vedi,\ le\ man\ giunte\ io\ stendo\ a\ te!$
Met music director Yannick Nézet-Séguin conducts. In August 2024 the Met extended his contract through 2029–30.
“All Rome trembled before him”: Tosca delivers it on one note, a middle C-sharp monotone, sometimes simply spoken.
Act III opens with a 16-bar horn theme. Remember it: the lovers will sing it in their final duet.
These matins bells were researched: Puccini went to Castel Sant’Angelo to hear how they sound from its ramparts.
De Tommaso grew up hearing Pavarotti in his family’s restaurant. Pavarotti’s last stage role: Cavaradossi, here, in 2004.
A somber clarinet solo opens “E lucevan le stelle”, in B minor.
Puccini insisted on the words “muoio disperato” (I die in despair), and declined advice to bin the aria.
Ricordi wanted a transcendent love duet here. Puccini’s defense: Tosca is busy teaching Mario to feign death.
The final bars: the “E lucevan le stelle” theme returns tutta forza, as loudly as possible.
